error.message: name must be 1-64 characters of [A-Za-z0-9._-], must not start with '.', and must not contain '..'

BadRequest.description: Validation failure; error.code disambiguates (invalid_name, invalid_path, unknown_project, project_path_missing, path_and_project, bad_request).

OriginForbidden.description: Cross-origin request on a mutating route.

UnsupportedMediaType.description: POST body was not declared application/json.

code.description: Stable machine-readable code from the registry in the top-level description. Clients switch on this, never on message.

apiPath.description: Prefix every route in this document below `/api/v1` is served under — append the route's remainder to it, so `/api/v1/sessions` is `apiPath + "/sessions"`. Always `/api/v1` today, and the counterpart to `terminalPath`: the two move together if a deployment is ever put behind a path prefix, and reading both is what keeps a client working when they do. Note the scope — it covers the versioned API only, and says nothing about `/token`, `/healthz`, `/openapi.json`, `/docs/` or `/`, which are not below it and are not described by it.

features.description: Capability strings from the registry in the top-level description. Clients MUST ignore unknown entries and MUST feature-detect anything beyond the ttyd-compatible core before using it — this list is the only cross-repo skew defense that exists.

hostname.description: Short hostname of the machine serving this API.

maxSessionNameLength.description: The longest session name `POST /api/v1/sessions` will accept on **this** deployment. At most 64, and lower where the server's socket directory is deep enough to leave less room. Validate against this rather than against the schema pattern's 64, and rather than discovering it from a 400.

terminalPath.description: Path on this server to open the terminal WebSocket at — combine it with the server's host and port. Always `/ws` today; read it rather than hardcoding, so a future deployment behind a path prefix stays discoverable.

user.description: The service user — whose shell every terminal hands out.

exists.description: Whether `path` is currently a directory. False means a `POST` naming this project is refused with `project_path_missing` (400).

Session.description:
One session. How each field is derived, and how each can fail: `/docs/session-lifecycle.md` §2.

**Nulls are per-response, not sticky.** Every field is re-derived from the server's filesystem and process table on each request — nothing is cached — so a session reporting `cwd: null` or `pid: null` now may carry values on the next request, and the reverse. A null is never a permanent property of the session. It is equally not a promise that retrying helps: the usual cause is a process this server cannot inspect, and that persists for the session's lifetime. So do not poll specially and do not show a spinner waiting for a value to arrive — render the absence, and let your next ordinary refresh fill it in if it can.

agentStatus.description:
The last agent status this server observed on the session's own output, as defined by the in-band convention in `/docs/ws-protocol.md` §6a. Present only when `features` includes `session-status`.

**Null means unknown, and unknown is not idle.** Null says this server has never observed this session's output — no client has opened it through this server — so it is a statement about the server, not about the session. A session used only over SSH stays null forever, and every session is null after a restart until someone opens it. `clear` is the opposite kind of fact: the session itself reporting that it has nothing to report. Render the two differently, or a row nobody has looked at will claim nothing is happening.

**A status does not expire, so it can outlive what reported it.** §6a's limitation applies unchanged here: a state stands until something reports a different one, so an emitter killed rather than exited leaves `running` pinned. Do not add a timeout to work around this — §6a forbids clients inventing one, and the reasoning is there.

Ignore an unrecognized value rather than treating it as `clear`, so a server that learns a new state does not blank your indicator.

attached.description: True while someone is looking at this session — through this server or over SSH, so `true` does not imply a client of *this* server. That sentence is the contract. How it is worked out is not, and has already changed once, so clients MUST NOT derive it themselves and in particular MUST NOT read the socket's file mode. The derivation, and why it changed: `/docs/session-lifecycle.md` §2.

attachedCount.description:
How many viewers `attached` is counting — the same population, so this is `0` whenever `attached` is false, and at least `1` whenever it is true and this is not null.
Null means someone is attached and the server could not count them, which happens when the only evidence is dtach's own signalling and the viewer's process is not one this server can inspect. Treat it as "one or more", never as zero. Null is possible only while `attached` is true.
The counted case is best-effort rather than a census. Viewers connected through this server are exact. Viewers attached by other means are identified from the server's process table, which can miss one it is not allowed to inspect, and can briefly count a session's own supervising process while that session is shutting down. So use this to tell "just me" from "someone else as well"; do not build on an exact value, and do not treat a change in it as an event.
There is no way to ask which of these viewers is *you* — this server issues no client or connection identity, so nothing in this API could name one, and that is not planned. The usable substitute is arithmetic: a client that is itself attached to the session knows one of the count is its own, so `1` means it is alone and `2` or more means someone else is watching too.

createdAt.description: RFC 3339 UTC. Effectively when the session was created, but best-effort rather than forensic — treat it as ordering information, not evidence.

cwd.description: Current working directory of the session's shell, read live — it moves when the user `cd`s, so this is not the directory the session was created in. Null when it cannot be resolved; the session is still valid and still listed.

name.description:
Deliberately unconstrained here: a deep link creates names `POST` would reject, such as ones containing spaces, and this API lists every session that exists. Do not validate a listed name against the create-side pattern.
Always valid UTF-8, and never contains `/` — a name is a filename component on the server, so one cannot occur. That matters because this string is the byte-exact key for `GET` and `DELETE` on `/api/v1/sessions/{name}`: round-trip it unchanged, URL-encoding as the transport requires, and it will always match.

pid.description: PID of the session's shell — the same process whose `cwd` is reported above. Null when it cannot be resolved; the session is still valid and still listed.

SessionCreateRequest.description: `path` and `project` are mutually exclusive; omitting both means the service user's $HOME. Unknown extra properties are ignored (a newer client against an older server degrades predictably; capability discovery is /api/v1/meta's job, not schema strictness here).

name.description: Stricter than the deep-link path on purpose: a name MUST NOT start with `.` — its socket would be a hidden file in the session directory — and MUST NOT contain `..` anywhere, because such a session would exist but could never be reached by deep link. A deep link accepts both, so a session listed here may have either; only creation through this endpoint is restricted. The pattern's 64-character ceiling is an **upper bound only** — a deployment may accept fewer and refuses the excess with `invalid_name` (400), whose `detail` names the real figure. Clients SHOULD surface that `detail` rather than assume 64.

path.description: Absolute directory to start the shell in. Must exist, must be a directory, and must not contain bytes below 0x20 or 0x7F — those are refused with `invalid_path` (400) rather than escaped.

TerminalHandshake.description: The first message on a `/ws` connection, and the only one with no opcode prefix. Sent as either a text or a binary frame. See the `/ws` description for the framing that applies to everything after it.

AuthToken.description: The value from `GET /token`, which is always the empty string here. Accepted and ignored; may be omitted entirely. Spelled with this capitalisation for ttyd parity.

columns.description: Terminal width. Applied before the session's command starts, so this is the width it first renders at. Omitted or out of range silently means 80 — which on a narrow client produces a wrapped, unusable screen with no error, so send the real value.

rows.description: Terminal height. Omitted or out of range silently means 24.

TerminalResize.description: Payload of a `RESIZE_TERMINAL` frame (opcode `'1'`). Applied immediately, one per frame, never coalesced. Out-of-range values cause the frame to be ignored, not the connection to close.

externalDocs.description: The WebSocket protocol, the session model, and the ttyd compatibility matrix — served by this binary at /docs/, so this reference resolves for any reader that can reach the API.

info.description:
## Security model — read before adding anything

This service fronts a **writable, unauthenticated shell** running as the service
user. There is **no authentication at any layer of this API, by design** — access
control is the network interface the daemon binds to (a tailnet IP, `127.0.0.1`,
or a specific interface; wtd refuses `0.0.0.0`/`::` even when explicitly
configured). Every endpoint below is reachable by anyone who can reach the port.
The question for any change to this file: *does it widen who can reach the shell?*

## CSRF and cross-origin policy (normative for every route)

Because there is no auth, the classic CSRF mitigations-by-credential do not exist;
any web page a user visits can attempt requests against a tailnet IP. Therefore:

- **Mutating routes** (`POST`, `DELETE`) reject any request carrying an `Origin`
  header whose authority (host[:port]) differs from the request's `Host`
  authority → `403` with code `origin_forbidden`. `Origin` is the **only** header
  consulted: `Referer`, `Sec-Fetch-Site` and `Sec-Fetch-Mode` are never read, so
  setting them changes nothing. The comparison is case-insensitive and ignores the
  scheme, so only the authority has to match. Three outcomes, exhaustively:

  | `Origin` on the request | result |
  |---|---|
  | absent, or present but empty | **accepted** — native clients (the iOS app's URLSession) send none |
  | authority equals `Host` | **accepted** — wtd's own picker pages are same-origin |
  | anything else, including the literal `null` | **403** `origin_forbidden` |

  The `null` row is the one worth planning for, because a client does not always
  choose its own `Origin`: sandboxed iframes, `file://` documents and some WebView
  configurations have `Origin: null` forced on them by the engine. Such a context
  cannot call the mutating routes at all, and no request header will change that —
  use a native HTTP client, which sends no `Origin`, or serve your page from wtd
  itself so it is same-origin. Reverse proxies must preserve the original `Host`
  header or this check will reject legitimate browsers.
- **`POST` routes** additionally require `Content-Type: application/json`
  → `415` with code `unsupported_media_type` otherwise. HTML forms cannot send
  `application/json`, which kills form-based CSRF outright.
- wtd **never** sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` — or any CORS headers at
  all on `/api/*`. CORS headers exist to *grant* cross-origin access; this API
  must never grant it. So a browser-based client cannot call this API from another
  origin and no header will change that: serve your page from wtd itself (`GET /`),
  or use a native client, which sends no `Origin` and is unaffected.
- Request bodies are capped at 16 KiB → `413` with code `payload_too_large`.
- The same Origin policy applies to the `/ws` upgrade itself — see
  `/docs/ws-protocol.md` section 12; a cross-site WebSocket is a cross-site shell. One
  difference on that path: the rejection comes from the WebSocket layer before any handler
  runs, so it is a plain-text `403`, **not** the JSON `Error` object every route below
  returns. Do not try to parse a body for `origin_forbidden` there — the status is the
  whole signal.

Residual exposure, stated honestly: the Origin-vs-Host comparison stops ordinary
cross-site requests (Origin names the attacker's site, Host names this server —
mismatch, rejected). It does **not** stop DNS rebinding, where the victim's
browser requests `http://attacker-hostname:7681/...` after the attacker's DNS
flips to this IP — then Origin and Host both name the attacker's hostname, they
match each other, and the check passes, `/ws` included. The only complete fix is
validating `Host` against an allowlist; a `WT_ALLOWED_HOSTS` config key is
reserved for that and deliberately **not** in v1, because unconfigured it would
break tailnet MagicDNS names and raw-IP access, and a misconfigured allowlist
locks the owner out of their own box. What contains rebinding meanwhile is the
precondition it needs: the victim's *browser* must itself be on the private
network this daemon binds to. That is the repo's standing security stance — the
service is exactly as private as the interface it binds to — restated, not
weakened.

**There is no client-side action here, and that is deliberate.** Rebinding
targets a browser the attacker lures to a page they control; it does not target
your client, and nothing a legitimate client sends changes the outcome. In
particular, connecting by raw IP rather than a tailnet MagicDNS name neither helps
nor hurts — the check compares `Origin` against whatever `Host` you sent, so both
are accepted and neither is the safer choice. Use whichever is convenient. The
mitigation, if this deployment ever needs one, is server-side (`WT_ALLOWED_HOSTS`)
and would be announced as a feature flag.

## Path behavior outside this spec

- `GET /` serves HTML: with no `?arg=` query parameter, the **browser session
  picker** (lists dtach sessions, links to `/?arg=<name>`); with `?arg=` present
  (even empty), the **terminal page**, whose script opens
  `ws://<host>/ws + location.search` exactly as ttyd's bundled client does. Pages
  use relative URLs so they work behind a path-stripping reverse proxy.
- `GET /ws` is the terminal WebSocket — the entire contract is
  `ws-protocol.md`. It appears below only as a stub so the path is not "free".
- Unknown paths → `404` with the standard error object. Known paths with wrong
  methods → `405`, code `method_not_allowed`.
- All `/api/*` and `/token` responses carry `Cache-Control: no-store`.

## Error object

Every non-2xx response from `/token`, `/healthz`, and `/api/*` is the `Error`
schema: `{"error": {"code": "...", "message": "...", "detail": "..."}}`. `code`
is a stable machine-readable string from the registry below (clients switch on
`code`, never on `message`); `message` is one human-readable sentence; `detail`
is optional elaboration. The registry is open-ended — clients MUST treat unknown
codes as opaque failures of the given HTTP status.

| code | HTTP | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `bad_request` | 400 | Body is not a JSON object, or violates the schema in a way not covered below. |
| `invalid_name` | 400 | Session name fails the create-side rules, including a deployment-specific length ceiling that `detail` states. |
| `invalid_path` | 400 | `path` is not absolute, contains control bytes, does not exist, or is not a directory. |
| `unknown_project` | 400 | `project` names no entry in the projects file. |
| `project_path_missing` | 400 | Project exists but its path does not; the API refuses to guess a fallback. |
| `path_and_project` | 400 | Both `path` and `project` were supplied; they are mutually exclusive. |
| `already_exists` | 409 | A session with this name already exists, including one whose death could not be established — it is reported rather than silently replaced. |
| `not_found` | 404 | No such session / no such route. |
| `origin_forbidden` | 403 | Cross-origin request on a mutating route (or the /ws upgrade). |
| `unsupported_media_type` | 415 | POST without `Content-Type: application/json`. |
| `payload_too_large` | 413 | Body over 16 KiB. |
| `method_not_allowed` | 405 | Known path, wrong method. |
| `internal` | 500 | Unexpected server fault; `detail` says what, socket state untouched unless stated. |

## What "ttyd-compatible" means here

Every compatibility claim in this document — the `/ws` wire protocol, `GET /token`,
`?arg=` handling, the `-W` and `-a` behaviours — is against **ttyd 1.7.4**, and no
other release: <https://github.com/tsl0922/ttyd/releases/tag/1.7.4>. The version is
load-bearing rather than incidental, because ttyd's wire protocol is not stable
across releases; a client author whose fallback is reading ttyd's source needs to
know *which* source, and a client tested against a different ttyd may be testing
against a different protocol. Where wtd deliberately diverges from 1.7.4,
`/docs/compatibility.md` lists it row by row.

## Features registry (`GET /api/v1/meta`)

The `features` array is the **anti-skew mechanism** between this repo and the iOS
client: the two repos share no CI, no type checking, and installed phone builds
do not update when the server does. A client MUST feature-detect any capability
beyond the ttyd-compatible core (`/`, `/ws`, `/token`) by checking this list, and
MUST ignore feature strings it does not recognize.

| feature | meaning |
|---|---|
| `token` | `GET /token` served (ttyd compat). |
| `url-arg` | `?arg=` is appended to the start command argv (always on in wtd). |
| `writable` | Terminal input is accepted (always on in wtd; ttyd `-W`). |
| `sessions-api` | `GET/POST /api/v1/sessions`, `DELETE /api/v1/sessions/{name}`. |
| `projects-api` | `GET /api/v1/projects`. |
| `picker-ui` | `GET /` serves the HTML picker when no `?arg=` is present. |
| `scrollback-replay` | A named (`?arg=`) connection is sent the session's recent output on attach, before live output. |
| `docs-endpoint` | `GET /docs/{file}` serves the documents this spec references, so every reference in it resolves. |
| `session-read` | `GET /api/v1/sessions/{name}` reads one session, so the `Location` header a create returns is fetchable. |
| `session-status` | A session carries `agentStatus`: what the agent running in it last reported about itself. |

**A flag's meaning never narrows, so gate on the flag that names what you want.**
`sessions-api` covers list, create and delete as one unit; this server has no mode
in which some of the three work and others do not, so do not probe them
independently. If one ever does become independently optional it gets its own flag
*alongside* `sessions-api`, which keeps meaning all three — the way `session-read`
was added for `GET /api/v1/sessions/{name}` rather than folded into the existing
flag. Two consequences for a client: a capability you cannot find a flag for is one
this document does not offer yet, not one you should feature-test by calling it; and
an unrecognized flag is always additive, so ignoring it is always safe.

**`sessions-api` will not be withdrawn, and clients are entitled to rely on that.** The
primary client treats a server that answers but does not advertise it as an *error* — it
shows "Not a wtd Server", offers Retry, and names SSH as the recovery path — rather than
falling back to a bare terminal. That degraded mode was removed deliberately, so dropping
the flag from a future server would not degrade those clients, it would lock them out. The
same is not true of `session-read`, which is genuinely optional: a client that misses it
falls back to list-and-filter.

Reserved for the future (a server advertising one implements its spec revision):
`auth-basic`, `base-path`, `tls`, `flow-control`.
info.summary: Browser terminal daemon: ttyd-wire-compatible WebSocket terminal plus a JSON API over dtach sessions.
info.title: wtd HTTP API

get.description:
HTML, not API. Without `arg`: the browser session picker. With `arg` (even
empty): the terminal page, which forwards its full query string to `/ws`,
matching ttyd's own client — so a deep link opens the named session directly.

parameters.description: Session name to deep-link. A malformed or unusable name opens a plain shell instead — a graceful fallback, never an error. The page forwards this to `/ws` unchanged, so the rules there apply verbatim.
parameters.name: arg

get.summary: Browser picker (no ?arg=) or terminal page (?arg= present)

get.description:
The anti-skew endpoint (see the features registry in the top-level description). Call
it once each time you connect to a server and cache it no longer than that: it is cheap,
and the whole point is noticing a server that changed underneath an installed client.
Caching across app launches defeats the purpose.

The shortcuts this deployment has configured, already parsed — a client never
reads the file itself. Each entry reports `exists`, whether its path is
currently a directory, so a client can warn before creating a session
somewhere unexpected. A deployment with no shortcuts configured, or an
unreadable file, is an empty list rather than an error.

Every session this server can see, sorted ascending by the byte value of `name`. Sessions
can be created by deep link as well as by `POST`, and every surface that lists them must
agree about what exists — which drives both rules below.

1. **Looser names than this API would create are still listed.** A session made by
   deep-linking `/ws?arg=my%20proj` is named `my proj`; it appears here even though
   `POST` would reject that name. Do not assume listed names satisfy the create-side
   pattern. Names beginning with `.` are listed too, even though `POST` refuses them.
2. **Dead sessions are not listed, and this request removes them.** A socket
   left behind by a session that is gone would otherwise show as a session
   that cannot be attached, so this endpoint verifies each one and unlinks the
   ones it can prove are dead. That probing is also why this read is not instant:
   budget a client timeout of a few seconds rather than a few hundred milliseconds, and
   expect the cost to grow with the number of sessions. Yes, that means a `GET` has a
   side effect; it is
   the only read every client already makes, which is why it is the one that
   converges what exists with what is listed. Why, and the guard against racing a
   session being recreated under the same name: `/docs/session-lifecycle.md` §5.

post.description:
Creates a dtach session **without attaching**, for naming a working directory or
project up front. It is **not** a precondition for deep-linking: `/ws?arg=<name>`
creates the session if it does not exist, so a client can open one directly and never
call this.

A session created here is **indistinguishable** from one created by deep link — same
invocation, same environment, built from the same code. That parity is mandatory, so
anything you can do with a deep-linked session you can do with this one, and nothing
about it will surprise a user who switches between the two.
The invocation and the reasons each part of it matters: `/docs/session-lifecycle.md` §6.

Working directory: `project` (a shortcut name from `GET /api/v1/projects`) or
`path` (absolute, must exist), else the service user's `$HOME`. The two are
mutually exclusive. Where a deep-linked connection silently falls back to `$HOME`
for a directory that is missing, this API returns an error instead — a program
should be told, not guessed for.

Name rules are **stricter than the deep-link path's**, deliberately: no leading `.`
and no `..` anywhere, the latter because such a session could never be reached by
deep link. See the `name` property for the length ceiling, which is
deployment-dependent.

If the name belongs to a session that is already gone, its leftover socket is
removed and creation proceeds — so retrying a create for a session that has
died does the obvious thing rather than returning a conflict.

Location.description: Canonical resource path for the new session.

409.description: A session with this name already exists. Two concurrent creates of the same name resolve to one winner and one 409. A session whose death cannot be established counts as existing, and is reported rather than silently replaced.

delete.description:
Terminates the session and removes its socket; `204` once the socket is gone.

**No path is ever constructed from `{name}`** — it is URL-decoded and matched
byte-exact against the names that actually exist. That is why this parameter
has no validation pattern: a deep link creates names `POST` would reject, and those
sessions must be deletable too. A name matching nothing is `404`, including anything
containing `/`.

Deleting an **attached** session is allowed. The live shell is terminated under
whoever is watching it, and their connection closes normally rather than erroring;
this API does not guess whether that is what you meant.
Deleting a session that is **already gone** also succeeds → `204`, including one
that has become unreachable by every other route, so `DELETE` is the way to
clean up after a session nothing else can address.

The session's background jobs are terminated along with it. Termination is
bounded at roughly **7 s** worst case — budget a client timeout above that —
which is why this endpoint answers synchronously instead of handing back a job
to poll. Ordering, escalation, and the phantom-session failure modes the
ordering exists to prevent: `/docs/session-lifecycle.md` §7.

parameters.description: Exact session name as returned by a list response, URL-encoded as needed.
parameters.name: name

204.description: Session terminated and its socket removed.

404.description: No socket with this name exists.

500.description: Termination did not complete inside the bounded ~7 s. The session is left as it was and is still listed, so a retry is safe.

delete.summary: Terminate a session and clean up its socket

get.description: The same object the list returns, for one name — this is what the `Location` header on a `201` points at. `{name}` is URL-decoded and matched byte-exact against the names that exist, so a name the list shows is always fetchable even when it would fail the create-side rules. Detect with the `session-read` feature; a server without it forces a list-and-filter instead.

parameters.description: Exact session name as returned by a list response, URL-encoded as needed.
parameters.name: name

404.description: No session with this name exists.

get.description: The documents this spec references, served so those references resolve. OpenAPI cannot express a WebSocket protocol, so `/docs/ws-protocol.md` is where the terminal's wire contract is stated in full; `/docs/session-lifecycle.md` carries the session model and `/docs/compatibility.md` the ttyd behaviour matrix. Markdown, intended to be read. Detect with the `docs-endpoint` feature.

parameters.description: One of the published document names.
parameters.name: file

get.summary: A specification document this server publishes

get.description: Liveness for systemd, scripts, and humans with curl. Returns `{"status": "ok"}` when the HTTP listener is serving, and deliberately checks nothing deeper — not sessions, not the start command. A health check that can fail for reasons a restart will not fix trains people to ignore it.
HTML, not API. A short FAQ for people using the browser terminal — keyboard gotchas, disconnect behaviour, session sharing. The terminal page shows the same document in its "?" overlay.

The machine-readable contract, served by the binary that implements it so a client (or a person with curl) can inspect exactly what this build speaks. Rendered from api/openapi.yaml at build time; the served document and the repo file must not drift.

Exists solely because clients of ttyd expect it: they GET it on every connect,
ignore failures, and send the result as the handshake `AuthToken`. wtd has no
auth, so the token is always the empty string — the same as ttyd run without
`-c`. Serving it keeps connect logs clean and third-party ttyd-compatible
clients working.

Not an HTTP resource in any REST sense — this path upgrades to the ttyd
`tty`-subprotocol WebSocket. OpenAPI cannot express a WebSocket protocol, so what
follows is the working contract in prose. It is enough to build a client; the full
normative version, including every failure mode, is `/docs/ws-protocol.md`.

## Connecting

Open `ws://<host>:<port>/ws`, offering subprotocol `tty`. The server echoes it, which
browsers require. Offering **none** also works and the connection proceeds with no
subprotocol selected; offering others **without** `tty` is a `400` before the upgrade,
so check the status rather than waiting for a close code. `GET /token` first if you want ttyd parity — its value goes in the handshake —
but the token here is always the empty string.

## The handshake

The **first** message after the upgrade is the handshake, and it is the one message with
**no opcode prefix**. Send `TerminalHandshake` as **either a text or a binary** frame;
both are accepted, which matters because ttyd's own web client sends binary and other
clients send text.

Send real `columns`/`rows`, as **numbers**. Missing or out-of-range values (outside
**1..65535**) default to **80x25 silently**, and the size is applied before the start
command runs — so a narrow client that omits them gets a session hard-wrapped for 80
columns with no error anywhere. A dimension that is not a number at all (`"80"`, `80.5`,
`true`) is not defaulted: it makes the payload undecodable and closes **1002**.

Unknown keys are ignored. Not-JSON closes **1002**; no handshake within **10 s** closes
**1008**; over **8 KiB** closes **1009**.

## Framing, after the handshake

Every subsequent message is `[1 ASCII opcode byte][payload]`, applied to the reassembled
message rather than to transport fragments.

| Client → server | Byte | Payload |
|---|---|---|
| `INPUT` | `'0'` | Raw bytes, written to the terminal verbatim. No escaping, no encoding. |
| `RESIZE_TERMINAL` | `'1'` | `TerminalResize` as JSON. |
| `PAUSE` / `RESUME` | `'2'` / `'3'` | Accepted for ttyd parity and **no-ops here**; see the `flow-control` feature. |

| Server → client | Byte | Payload |
|---|---|---|
| `OUTPUT` | `'0'` | Raw terminal bytes. |
| `SET_WINDOW_TITLE` | `'1'` | UTF-8 string; display verbatim, nothing parses it. |
| `SET_PREFERENCES` | `'2'` | JSON, always `{}` here. |

Client messages may be text or binary. **Server messages are always binary.**

## Three rules that silently corrupt rendering

1. **The first two server frames are the title and the preferences**, in that order,
   before any output. Feed them to a terminal emulator and it prints them on screen.
2. **`OUTPUT` is not UTF-8-safe per frame.** A multi-byte character can split across two
   frames. Decode the concatenated stream, never one frame at a time, or non-ASCII output
   corrupts intermittently at frame boundaries.
3. **Ignore unknown opcodes; do not close on them.** New opcodes may appear, and a client
   that treats byte 0 as an error never gets past its first frame. The server ignores
   unknown client opcodes for the same reason.

## Two kinds of connection, chosen by `?arg=` alone

Nothing else on the wire differs.

| | argless `/ws` | named `/ws?arg=<name>` |
|---|---|---|
| Process | fresh per connection, private shell | one shared session, kept alive between connections |
| On attach | a new shell prompt | recent output replayed, then live |
| A second client | gets its own shell | joins the same terminal, **input interleaves** |
| You disconnect | the process is terminated | **the session keeps running** |

`?arg=<name>` **creates the session if it does not exist** and recovers one whose previous
process is gone — so a saved deep link works before its session has ever existed, and
after a reboot. You do not need to `POST` first.

An **empty** `?arg=` counts as argless: no replay, no sharing, and the process dies with
the connection. Build the URL without the parameter rather than with an empty one.

**An argless connection is not how you browse sessions.** It is a plain shell in the
service user's home directory, with no session behind it — nothing to reattach to later.
Use `GET /api/v1/sessions` to list, and `?arg=<name>` to open one.

A name that cannot be used still opens a working terminal — never an error, never a close.
See the `arg` parameter for exactly what that terminal is.

**Ctrl-`\` is shared fate on a named session.** It detaches the session, which closes
**every** client attached to it, not only the one that sent it. Indistinguishable from a
private detach when you are the only client.

## Resize, and the redraw you should not send

Every `RESIZE_TERMINAL` frame is applied immediately, one per frame, never coalesced —
so debouncing an interactive resize is your job. Dimensions outside 1..65535 are ignored
rather than fatal. With several clients on one session the size is last-writer-wins:
joining a session resizes it for everyone already there.

**You do not need to send a resize to get output**, and you should not send a
size-jiggle to force a redraw. This server performs that once per session itself. A
client-side jiggle still works but repaints the screen for **every** client on a shared
session. This is the one rule that inverts against a plain ttyd server, which does no
redraw of its own and where a client-side jiggle is the only thing preventing a blank
screen on attach — so gate it on the `scrollback-replay` feature rather than assuming.

## Replay, when `scrollback-replay` is advertised

Recent output is replayed after the title and preferences frames, before live output.
It arrives as **ordinary `OUTPUT` frames with no marker of any kind** — deliberately, so
that a client which knows nothing about replay still works. Consequences:

- **You cannot detect where replay ends.** Do not try.
- **It overlaps whatever you already have** if you reconnect into a terminal emulator you
  kept alive. Clearing before reconnecting is your decision; the server injects nothing.
- **It is wrapped at the width of the session that produced it**, not yours. A narrow
  client joining a wide session sees history wrapped for the wide one. Full-screen
  programs repaint; a shell's scrollback does not.
- **Do not depend on it to render a usable screen.** An operator can disable it while the
  feature stays advertised.

Replay covers what happened *before* you attached; your own scrollback covers what
arrived *while* you were connected. Different mechanisms, both needed.

## Liveness

**You do not have to ping** — browsers cannot, so the server never treats silence from a
client as death. It pings every 30 s and closes after **three consecutive pings go
unanswered**, so a live connection has 90 s of tolerance and a single lost pong costs
nothing. Transport-level auto-pong satisfies this for free: browsers and URLSession both
answer without any code of yours, which is why an idle terminal survives indefinitely.

What is consulted is the **pong**, not traffic in general — sending input does not by
itself keep a connection alive if your transport is not answering pings. No real client
is in that position, and a hand-rolled one that suppresses pongs is the case to know
about. There is no idle timeout below 60 s. The server answers pings with pongs and
ignores unsolicited pongs.

## Limits

Any message after the handshake over **1 MiB** closes **1009**. That is the ceiling on a
single paste. It is unrelated to the 16 KiB cap on HTTP request bodies documented above.

What else it takes down depends on the connection shape. On an **argless** connection the
process is yours alone and dies with you. On a **named** one only your client is dropped —
the session keeps running for every other client, so reconnecting lands you back in it with
replay. One client's oversized paste cannot end a session someone else is using.

## Close codes, and what to do about each

| Code | Means | Do |
|---|---|---|
| `1000` | The session's command exited. On a named session this is the shared command, so every client gets it. | Final. Reconnect only if the user asks. |
| `1001` | Server shutting down, or a warm session released to make room. Sent on **named** connections; an argless one is dropped without a close frame on shutdown. | Reconnect with backoff. Sessions survive a restart. |
| `1013` | You fell more than 4 MiB behind on output and were dropped so the session could keep going. | Reconnect immediately; replay restores context. |
| `1002` | The first message was not a valid handshake. | Client bug. Do not retry. |
| `1008` | No handshake within 10 s. | Client bug. Do not retry. |
| `1009` | A message exceeded 8 KiB (handshake) or 1 MiB (after). | Client bug. The same payload fails identically. |
| `1011` | The terminal could not be started. The title and preferences frames arrive first, then an `OUTPUT` frame with a one-line error, so the reason is visible in the terminal rather than only in a code. | Retry with backoff — but display the message. The commonest cause is a misconfigured start command, which fails the same way every time. |

`TERM=xterm-256color` is set, so xterm-family emulation is the target.

parameters.description:
Session name. Present and non-empty selects a named connection, creating the session if it does not exist; absent or empty selects a private one. Repeats are passed through in order, though only the first is used today. URL-decoded before use.
A name this server cannot build a session from does not fail the connection: it opens a plain shell instead, preceded by one `OUTPUT` line beginning `wtd:` that says why. **No value of `arg` closes the connection.** Two kinds of unusable name behave differently afterwards, and the difference is observable if a second client deep-links the same name:
*Unusable as a session, still a name.* One containing `/` or `..`, and one whose socket path would exceed the operating system's limit. No session is created, but the connection remains a *named* one for sharing and replay — so two clients on the same unusable name land on **one shared fallback shell**, and both see the explanation.
*Not carriable at all, so discarded.* A value containing a NUL byte (`%00`) or over **4096 bytes**. These cannot be carried as a process argument, so the server drops them before choosing a session. Separately, only the first **16 usable** values are kept and any beyond that are ignored — counted after the unusable ones are removed, so sending one NUL does not cost a usable value its place. A connection whose only `arg` was dropped is therefore **argless**: private shell, no sharing, no replay, no explanation, and the process ends with the connection. Two clients doing it get one shell each.
Both are graceful; only the second loses the name, and only the first tells the user anything. Send a valid name if you want the sharing semantics.
The length ceiling is the one `POST /api/v1/sessions` enforces, so `maxSessionNameLength` from `GET /api/v1/meta` is a safe bound for both — validate against it before deep-linking, or your user gets a bare shell where they expected their session. Count **bytes of the UTF-8 encoding**, not characters: both the server and the operating system limit measure bytes, so a name that is short in characters and long in bytes is refused on the byte count. The reverse does not hold — this path accepts names `POST` would refuse, deliberately, so that a session created by any means can be reached by deep link.
Ignored repeats are dropped rather than refused, so a client cannot tell from the wire that it sent too many. Nothing legitimate sends more than one.
**Use the name exactly as `GET /api/v1/sessions` returned it.** That list is byte-exact, and this path accepts names `POST` would refuse — an interior space is legitimate and common (`my project`), and **leading or trailing whitespace is possible too**, because nothing between the URL and the socket name trims it. Trimming or normalising a name before putting it in `?arg=` therefore attaches to, or creates, a *different* session than the one the user picked. Round-trip it verbatim.
parameters.name: arg

101.description: Switching Protocols; subprotocol `tty` echoed when offered.

400.description: Not a valid upgrade, or subprotocols offered without `tty`.

servers.description:
wtd's single listener, and the only server that serves this document. host is the resolved bind address — a tailnet IP, 127.0.0.1, or an interface address, never a wildcard.
**Use port 7681 (`WT_PORT`).** One box runs one listener on one port, and it serves every route in this document. A server that answers `/`, `/token` and `/ws` but returns 404 for `/openapi.json`, the `/api/v1/*` routes and the picker is an older deployment that has not been upgraded; `GET /api/v1/meta` succeeding is the cheapest proof you are talking to wtd, and its `features[]` is how to test for anything newer than this revision.
